To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
non-synonymous substitutions at sites within CpG context, that is, sites with elevated mutation rate, are under a stronger selection.
hypermutable CpG sites are under stronger negative selection, which is revealed by the lower rate of evolution and the lower nucleotide diversity of these sites.
highly mutable CpG sites are under a strong negative selection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the rate of evolution and the strength of negative selection.
the impact of the CpG context on nucleotide mutation rates and on their fixation probability.
the interplay between mutation and selection and the role of CpG context in this interplay.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutation rate is not necessarily a good predictor of the strength of selection.
the probability that a mutation will have a phenotypic effect is independent of the rate of the mutation, but this statement is not necessarily true for all mutations.
the mutation rate and the effect of the mutation are not independent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mutation rate is not a random variable.
the mutation rate is not independent of the magnitude of the effect on fitness.
the hypermutable CpG context is a strong predictor of functional importance of a site.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mutation rate can affect the evolutionary trajectory of a sequence.
the mutation rate is not independent of the selection pressure at the nucleotide sites.
the rate of evolution of a nucleotide site depends not only on the rate of mutations but also on their effect on fitness.
